sentences.text: The only known fossil of Owenodon is a partial dentary, or lower jaw bone, discovered in the Lulworth Formation of the Purbeck Limestone Group. This holotype specimen, assigned the catalogue number NHMUK PV R 2998, dates to the middle Berriasian stage.
This animal lived approximately 143 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous period and belonged to the class Ornithischia.
The fossil bone was damaged during initial preparation but was successfully freed from the surrounding rock matrix in 1975.
The evolutionary position of Owenodon within ornithopod evolution remains uncertain due to the limited fossil material available for study.

The fossil was presented to the Natural History Museum in London in December 1901 and assigned the specimen number NHMUK PV R 2998. Richard Owen first described the species in 1874, originally assigning it to Iguanodon as I. hoggii.

Peter Galton established the genus Owenodon in 2009 after researchers questioned its placement in Camptosaurus. David Norman and Paul Barrett transferred the species to Camptosaurus in 2002, but Peter Galton established the genus Owenodon for it in 2009.
The fossil was found in the Cherty Freshwater Beds of the middle Purbeck at Durlston Bay, dating to the middle Berriasian age within the Tirnovella occitana zone.
Owenodon is classified within the family Iguanodontidae and the genus contains the single known species O. hoggii. The type species of the genus Owenodon is O. hoggii.

Galton interpreted Owenodon as a more derived iguanodontid than Camptosaurus but less derived than Lurdusaurus. Analyses by McDonald et al. from 2010 to 2017 found Owenodon to be an early member of Ankylopollexia. Herne et al. (2019) found Owenodon further from Iguanodon than Camptosaurus, either unresolved between Ankylopollexia and Dryosauridae or closer to Ankylopollexia.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Owenodon as Dryomorpha. Six fossil occurrences of Owenodon are recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
The time range for Owenodon is recorded as Tithonian to Berriasian, from 149.2 to 137.05 million years ago.

In 2002, David Norman and Paul Barrett reclassified the species as Camptosaurus hoggii based on similarities in tooth count and ridge structure. Kenneth Carpenter and Yvonne Wilson challenged the placement of the species in Camptosaurus in 2008, arguing it was more similar to Camptosaurus dispar than to the newly described Camptosaurus aphanoecetes. Greg Paul considered the species too incomplete to be placed in Camptosaurus and suggested it was an undiagnostic nomen dubium within Ornithopoda or Camptosauridae. David Norman considered the separation of Owenodon into its own genus to be provisional, arguing the decision was based more on stratigraphy and geography than on anatomical differences. In 2012, Peter Galton expanded the geographic range of Owenodon by adding a tooth from the El Castellar Formation of Spain, while removing most Romanian material from the genus. The species name hoggii was originally established by Owen in 1874. Owenodon hoggii is considered a taxon with inconsistent and uncertain classification.
